'''''Picea rubens''''', commonly known as '''red spruce''', is a species of [[spruce]] native to eastern North America, ranging from [[Nova Scotia]] to eastern [[Quebec]] and south-eastern [[Ontario]], and south through the [[Adirondack Mountains]] and [[New England]] along the [[Appalachians]] to [[western North Carolina]] and [[East Tennessee|eastern Tennessee]].<ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (1990). ''Pinaceae. Drawings and Descriptions of the Genera''. Koeltz Scientific Books {{ISBN|3-87429-298-3}}.</ref><ref name="fna">{{eFloras|1|233500913|Picea rubens |family=Pinaceae |first=Ronald J. |last=Taylor}}</ref><ref name=gd>{{Gymnosperm Database |family=Pinaceae |genus=Picea |species=rubens}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Red Spruce {{!}} Picea rubens |url=https://wildadirondacks.org/trees-of-the-adirondacks-red-spruce-picea-rubens.html |access-date=2025-10-01 |website=wildadirondacks.org |language=en}}</ref> This species is also known as '''yellow spruce, West Virginia spruce, eastern spruce,''' and '''he-balsam'''.<ref>{{Silvics |volume=1 |genus=Picea |species=rubens |first=Barton M. |last=Blum}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u7OVkfjEOAcC&pg=PA51 |title=A Natural History of Trees of Eastern and Central North America |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |date=1948-01-01 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin Harcourt |isbn=0-395-58174-5 |page=51|language=en}}</ref> Red spruce is the [[Provincial tree emblems of Canada|provincial tree]] of [[Nova Scotia]].<ref name="fna" />

== Description ==
[[File:Picea rubens cone.jpg|thumb|Foliage and cones]]

Red spruce is a perennial,<ref>{{cite web|title=Red Spruce (Rubens)|url=http://www.gardenguides.com/taxonomy/red-spruce-picea-rubens/|publisher=Garden Guides|access-date=27 February 2014|archive-date=17 February 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130217061621/http://www.gardenguides.com/taxonomy/red-spruce-picea-rubens/}}</ref> shade-tolerant, late successional<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dumais|first=D|author2=Prevost, M|title=Management for red spruce conservation in Quebec: The importance of some physiological and ecological characteristics – A review|journal=Forestry Chronicle|date=June 2007|volume=83|issue=3|pages=378–392|doi=10.5558/tfc83378-3|id={{ProQuest|294760995}}|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[conifer]]ous [[tree]] that under optimal conditions grows to {{convert|18|-|40|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall with a trunk diameter of about {{convert|60|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}, though exceptional specimens can reach {{convert|46|m|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|100|cm|in|0|abbr=in}} in diameter. It has a narrow conical crown. The [[leaf|leaves]] are needle-like, yellow-green, {{convert|12|-|15|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long, four-sided, curved, with a sharp point, and extend from all sides of the twig. The bark is gray-brown on the surface and red-brown on the inside, thin, and scaly. The wood is light, soft, has narrow rings, and has a slight red tinge.<ref>{{cite web|title=Red Spruce|url=https://plants.usda.gov/factsheet/pdf/fs_piru.pdf|publisher=USDA NRCS|access-date=26 February 2014}}</ref> The [[Conifer cone|cones]] are cylindrical, {{convert|3|-|5|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, with a glossy red-brown color and stiff scales. The cones hang down from branches.<ref name=farjon /><ref name=fna /><ref name=gd /><ref name=afc>{{cite web |website=A handbook of Maritime trees |publisher=Atlantic Forestry Centre |url=http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/maritimetrees/redspruce |title=Red Spruce |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080818060019/http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/subsite/maritimetrees/redspruce |archive-date=2008-08-18 }}</ref>

== Habitat ==
[[File:RedSpruceForestOnSpruceKnobWV.JPG|thumb|Dense red spruce forest in its native habitat at the summit of [[Spruce Knob]], [[West Virginia]]]]

Red spruce grows at a slow to moderate rate, lives for 250 to 450+ years, and is very shade-tolerant when young.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/~adk/oldlisteast/#spp |title = Eastern OLDLIST: A database of maximum tree ages for Eastern North America}}</ref> It is often found in pure stands or forests mixed with [[eastern white pine]], [[balsam fir]], or [[black spruce]]. Along with [[Fraser fir]], red spruce is one of two primary tree types in the [[southern Appalachian spruce-fir forest]], a distinct ecosystem found only in the highest elevations of the southern [[Appalachian Mountains]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |first=Peter |last=White |contribution=Boreal Forest |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Appalachia |publisher=University of Tennessee Press |date=2006 |pages=49–50}}</ref> Its habitat is moist but well-drained sandy [[loam]], often at high altitudes. Red spruce can be easily damaged by [[windthrow]] and [[acid rain]].

Notable red spruce forests in [[West Virginia]] can be seen at [[Gaudineer Scenic Area]], [[Canaan Valley]], [[Roaring Plains West Wilderness]], [[Dolly Sods Wilderness]], and [[Spruce Mountain (West Virginia)|Spruce Mountain]], all sites of former extensive red spruce forest.

== Related species ==
It is closely related to [[black spruce]], and [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] between the two are frequent where their ranges meet.<ref name=farjon /><ref name=fna /><ref name=gd /> Genetic data suggests that the red spruce [[peripatric speciation|peripatrically speciated]] from the black spruce during [[Glacial period|glaciation]] in the [[Pleistocene]].<ref name="Jaramillo-Correa and Bousquet">{{Citation |title=New evidence from mitochondrial DNA of a progenitor-derivative species relationship between black and red spruce (Pinaceae) |author=Juan P. Jaramillo-Correa & Jean Bousquet |journal=American Journal of Botany |year=2003 |volume=90 |issue=12 |pages=1801–1806 |doi= 10.3732/ajb.90.12.1801 |pmid=21653356}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Diverging patterns of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA diversity in subarctic black spruce: imprint of a founder effect associated with postglacial colonization |author=Isabelle Gamache, Juan P. Jaramillo-Correa, Sergey Payette, & Jean Bousquet |journal=Molecular Ecology |year=2003 |volume=12 |issue= 4|pages=891–901 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-294x.2003.01800.x|pmid=12753210 |bibcode=2003MolEc..12..891G |s2cid=20234158 }}</ref>

== Uses ==
Red spruce is used for [[Christmas tree]]s and is an important wood used in making [[Pulp (paper)|paper pulp]]. It is also an excellent [[tonewood]] and is used in many higher-end acoustic [[guitar]]s and [[Violin|violins]], as well as [[Sound board (music)|sound boards]]. The sap can be used to make [[spruce gum]].<ref name=afc /> Leafy red spruce twigs are boiled with sugar and flavoring to make [[spruce beer]]<ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=285}}</ref> or spruce pudding. It can be used as construction lumber and is good for [[Millwork (building material)|millwork]] and for crates.<ref>{{cite web| title=Red Spruce| url=http://www.wood-database.com/lumber-identification/softwoods/red-spruce/| publisher=The Wood Database| access-date=27 February 2014| archive-date=9 April 2014| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140409170821/http://www.wood-database.com/lumber-identification/softwoods/red-spruce/}}</ref>[[File:Nine picea rubens cones from Pisgah National Forest.jpg|thumb|Red spruce cones from the [[Pisgah National Forest]]]]

== Damaging factors ==
Like most trees, red spruce is subject to insect parasitism. Their insect enemy is the [[spruce budworm]], although it is a bigger problem for [[Picea glauca|white spruce]] and balsam fir.<ref>{{EOL|1033620|Red Spruce |access-date=27 February 2014}}</ref> Other issues that have been damaging red spruce have included the increase in acid rain and current climate change.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Houle|first=Daniel|title=Compositional vegetation changes and increased red spruce abundance during the Little Ice Age in a sugar maple forest of north-eastern North America|journal=Plant Ecology|year=2012|volume=213|issue=6|pages=1027–1035|doi=10.1007/s11258-012-0062-0|bibcode=2012PlEco.213.1027H |s2cid=15104515}}</ref>

One of the consequences of acid rain deposition is the decrease of soil exchangeable [[calcium]] and increase of [[Aluminium|aluminum]]. This is because acid precipitation disrupts [[Ion|cation]] and nutrition cycling in forest ecosystems. Components of acid rain such as [[Hydron (chemistry)|H<sup>+</sup>]], [[Nitrate|NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>]], and [[Sulfate|SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>]] limit the uptake of calcium by trees and can increase aluminum availability.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schaberg|first1=P. G.|last2=DeHayes|first2=D. H.|last3=Hawley|first3=G. J.|last4=Strimbeck|first4=G. R.|last5=Cumming|first5=J. R.|last6=Murakami|first6=P. F.|last7=Borer|first7=C. H.|date=2000-01-01|title=Acid mist and soil Ca and Al alter the mineral nutrition and physiology of red spruce|url=https://academic.oup.com/treephys/article/20/2/73/1702054|journal=Tree Physiology|language=en|volume=20|issue=2|pages=73–85|doi=10.1093/treephys/20.2.73|pmid=12651475|issn=0829-318X|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Calcium concentration is important for red spruce for physiological processes such as dark [[Respiration in plant|respiration]] and cold tolerance, as well as disease resistance, [[signal transduction]], [[Cell membrane|membrane]] and [[cell wall]] synthesis and function, and regulation of [[stoma]]ta. Conversely, dissolved aluminum can be toxic or can interfere with root uptake of calcium and other nutrients. At the [[ecosystem]] and [[Community (ecology)|community]] levels, Calcium availability is associated with community composition, mature tree growth, and ecosystem productivity. One study testing the effects of added aluminum to soil, found that ''P. rubens'' mortality rate increased under these conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kobe|first1=Richard K|last2=Likens|first2=Gene E|last3=Eagar|first3=Christopher|date=2002-06-01|title=Tree seedling growth and mortality responses to manipulations of calcium and aluminum in a northern hardwood forest|url=https://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/pdf/10.1139/x02-018|journal=Canadian Journal of Forest Research|volume=32|issue=6|pages=954–966|doi=10.1139/x02-018|issn=0045-5067|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

During the 1980s, increased acid deposition contributed to a loss of high-elevation red spruce trees caused by [[Soil leaching|leached]] calcium and thus decreased freezing tolerance.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Wason|first1=Jay W.|last2=Beier|first2=Colin M.|last3=Battles|first3=John J.|last4=Dovciak|first4=Martin|date=2019|title=Acidic Deposition and Climate Warming as Drivers of Tree Growth in High-Elevation Spruce-Fir Forests of the Northeastern US|journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change|language=en|volume=2|page=63 |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2019.00063|issn=2624-893X|doi-access=free|bibcode=2019FrFGC...2...63W }}</ref> Additionally, the structure of the spruce needle enhances the capture of water and particles, which has been shown to add to [[soil acidification]], nutrient leaching, and forest decline.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pierret|first1=Marie-Claire|last2=Viville|first2=Daniel|last3=Dambrine|first3=Etienne|last4=Cotel|first4=Solenn|last5=Probst|first5=Anne|date=2019-04-01|title=Twenty-five year record of chemicals in open field precipitation and throughfall from a medium-altitude forest catchment (Strengbach - NE France): An obvious response to atmospheric pollution trends|journal=Atmospheric Environment|language=en|volume=202|pages=296–314|doi=10.1016/j.atmosenv.2018.12.026|bibcode=2019AtmEn.202..296P|issn=1352-2310|doi-access=free}}</ref> However, more recently, reductions in acid deposition have contributed to red spruce resurgence in some mountain areas in the northeastern United States. This increase in red spruce growth has been associated with an increase in rainfall [[pH]], which reduces bulk acidic deposition. This suggests that policies aiming to reduce atmospheric pollution in this area have been effective, although other species sensitive to soil acidification, such as [[Acer saccharum|sugar maple]], are still continuing to decline.<ref name=":0" />

== Conservation ==
The red spruce has low genetic diversity as well as a narrow ecological niche, meaning the tree is easily susceptible to changes within its environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parmar |first1=Rajni |last2=Cattonaro |first2=Federica |last3=Phillips |first3=Carrie |last4=Vassiliev |first4=Serguei |last5=Morgante |first5=Michele |last6=Rajora |first6=Om P. |date=2022-12-03 |title=Assembly and Annotation of Red Spruce (Picea rubens) Chloroplast Genome, Identification of Simple Sequence Repeats, and Phylogenetic Analysis in Picea |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |volume=23 |issue=23 |article-number=15243 |doi=10.3390/ijms232315243 |issn=1422-0067|doi-access=free |pmid=36499570 |hdl=11390/1240084 |hdl-access=free |pmc=9739956 }}</ref> The Central Appalachian Spruce Restoration Initiative<ref>{{cite journal |last=Burks |first=Evan |date=Dec 2010 |url=http://www.wonderfulwv.com/sub.cfm?month=dec10&fea=1 |title=Return of the Red Spruce |journal=Wonderful West Virginia |volume=74 |issue=12 |pages=6–11}}</ref> seeks to unite diverse partners with the goal of restoring historic red spruce ecosystems across the high-elevation landscapes of central Appalachians. The partners that make up this diverse group are Appalachian Mountain Joint Venture, Appalachian Regional Reforestation Initiative, Canaan Valley National Wildlife Refuge, Natural Resources Conservation Service, [[The Mountain Institute]], [[The Nature Conservancy]], [[Trout Unlimited]], U.S. Forest Service Northern Research Station, U.S. Forest Service [[Monongahela National Forest]], West Virginia Division of Natural Resources, West Virginia Division of Forestry, West Virginia Highlands Conservancy, West Virginia State Parks, and West Virginia University.<ref>{{cite web|last=Bove|first=Jennifer|title=Appalachian Red Spruce Forest|url=http://endangeredspecies.about.com/od/endangeredspecieshabitats/a/Appalachian-Red-Spruce-Forest.htm|access-date=27 February 2014|archive-date=12 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140412224201/http://endangeredspecies.about.com/od/endangeredspecieshabitats/a/Appalachian-Red-Spruce-Forest.htm}}</ref>

Prior to the late 19th century, {{convert|600,000|ha}} of red spruce were in West Virginia. In the late 19th and early 20th century, a vast amount of logging began in the state, and the number of red spruce dwindled to {{convert|12,000|ha}}. [[Silviculture]] is being used to help restore the population of the lost red spruce.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rentch|first=James|author2=T. Schuler |author3=M. Ford |author4=G. Nowacki |title=Red Spruce Stand Dynamics, Simulations, and Restoration Opportunities in the Central Appalachians|journal=Restoration Ecology|date=September 2007|volume=15|issue=3|pages=440–452|doi=10.1111/j.1526-100x.2007.00240.x|bibcode=2007ResEc..15..440R |s2cid=85913515 |id={{ProQuest|289371889}}}}</ref>

Significant efforts have been made to increase the growth of red spruce trees in [[western North Carolina]], most notably by Molly Tartt on behalf of the [[Daughters of the American Revolution]] (DAR). Tartt embarked on a mission to find the lost red spruce forest that had been planted by the DAR as a memorial to the lives lost during the [[American Revolution]]. The forest, consisting of 50,000 trees was dedicated in 1940 and had until recently been forgotten until Tartt located and identified the forest near [[Devil's Courthouse]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://smokymountainnews.com/archives/item/18661-daughters-of-the-american-revolution-brings-forgotten-forest-to-light#:~:text=The%20N.C.%20Daughters%20in%20responded%20well%20above%20the,a%20bronze%20tablet.%20But%20the%20recognition%20was%20short-lived | title=Daughters of the American Revolution brings forgotten forest to light }}</ref>
